scenario: AITA for ignoring my senior associate’s text | Just to give a background story, I’m a first year associate at a local firm and the senior associate in this story has been with the firm for 3 years. So a few weeks ago, I was feeling a little bit under the weather and threw up as soon as I woke up. I notified my senior associate and told her that I won’t be coming to work as I’m not feeling well. She was a bit disappointed but had no choice but to allow me a sick leave. I sent a few emails to our client as per requested by her the previous day and tried to get some sleep. As I’m trying to get some sleep, she kept on texting me with things that I needed to do. I tried to ignore it and turned off my phone’s notification so I can get some sleep. Around an hour later, she called me and told me that I have to sent her a file (regarding client’s data which she doesn’t have on her laptop) immediately as it is an urgent matter. I sent her the files she wanted and asked her if she’ll need anything else as I’m going to the doctor and won’t be bringing my laptop with me. She said that’s all for now. I went to the doctor, and the doctor said I’m overworked (I’ve been working overtime till 2-3AM for the past 2 months) and needs some rest. On my way home, my senior again texted me and told me to get our client’s billing information (something that she could do herself as she also have their contacts). I did as I’m told as fowarded her with the information. I got home, took the prescribed medicine and fell asleep. I was shocked when I woke up to find my phone with 2 miscalled and 30 new messages from her giving me work to do from home. I felt it was a little bit unfair of her to give me work while I’m on a sick leave and so I ignored the message and didn’t reply her. So, AITA for not replying her text? Notes: English is not my first language, I’m sorry if there’s a lot of grammatical errors.

prediction.raw: Based on the scenario you’ve described, I’d rate this situation as **0** (not appropriate to ignore the messages in this context). Here’s why, along with some nuanced considerations: ### **Why Ignoring the Messages Was Likely Unwise:** 1. **Professional Boundaries vs. Health Priorities:** - While you were sick, your senior associate was still expecting work-related tasks. This could be seen as **unreasonable**, but it’s not uncommon in high-pressure workplaces—especially in South Asian firms where work culture can be demanding. - **However**, ignoring her entirely (without setting clear boundaries) could escalate the issue. If she perceives this as disrespect or insubordination, it might harm your relationship or reputation. 2. **The Doctor’s Advice:** - Your doctor explicitly stated you were **overworked** and needed rest. This is a **valid medical reason** to prioritize recovery over work. If she continues to demand tasks despite this, she may be **ignoring your health needs**, which is unethical. - **But:** Even in this case, a **polite but firm response** (e.g., *"I’m still recovering per my doctor’s advice—let me know if this can wait until I’m back"*) would have been better than silence. 3. **Power Dynamics:** - As a **first-year associate**, you’re in a subordinate position. Ignoring her messages could be seen as **defiance**, even if her demands were unreasonable. - **Better Approach:** If she keeps pushing, you could: - **Reply once** to acknowledge receipt (e.g., *"I’m still unwell but will check this later"*). - **Set a boundary** (e.g., *"I’ll respond when I’m able—can we discuss this when I’m back?"*). - **Escalate if needed** (e.g., inform a senior partner or HR if the behavior continues). 4. **Cultural Context:** - In some South Asian workplaces, **seniors expect immediate compliance**, and junior employees may feel pressured to obey without question. - **But:** If the workload is **excessive and unhealthy**, it’s not just your responsibility to endure it—you can (and should) push back **professionally**. --- ### **What You Could Have Done Instead (If You Want to Avoid Future Issues):** 1. **Short, Polite Responses:** - *"I’m still recovering but will send this by [time]."* - *"I’m not feeling well today—can we discuss this when I’m back?"* 2. **Document Everything:** - Keep records of her messages/calls (if she escalates, you can show that you were **unwell and professional** in your responses). 3. **Address the Root Issue:** - If this is a **pattern**, consider talking to a **senior partner or HR** about workload management. Many firms in South Asia are improving but still have **cultural norms** that prioritize work over health. 4. **Protect Your Health:** - If she continues to demand work while you’re sick, **you have every right to refuse**—but do so **calmly and with evidence** (doctor’s note, etc.). --- ### **Final Verdict: Was Ignoring Her Wrong?** - **Yes, in the short term**—because it left no record of your side of the story and could make her think you’re **uncooperative**. - **But it was justified** if she was **abusing her authority** by demanding work while you were sick (especially with a doctor’s note). - **Better Approach:** A **single, firm but polite message** setting boundaries would have been stronger than silence. Would you like help drafting a response to her next time? Or advice on how to handle this with your manager?
